title: Cloud Design Patterns
lesson: A pattern pairs a recurring problem with a design and the costs that come with it. Start with the constraint you can measure, such as a slow dependency or a burst of writes.
example: An image service can buffer a morning rush with a queue if people can wait for their thumbnails.
question: A team wants to add a queue to checkout. What should it establish first?
answers: Which work can finish after the customer gets a response
Which queue offers the longest retention
How many regions the broker supports
why: Moving work into a queue changes when users see the result. The team needs to know whether that delay fits the product.
detail: Sketch one user request, from the first click to the last durable write. Mark the step that fails your objective and name the improvement you need. If buffering makes a slow upload feel immediate, check how people learn when it has finished. That second question often reveals another piece of the design, such as a status endpoint.

terms.definition: An explicit limit, such as available memory, a delivery deadline or a cost ceiling.
An improvement in one property that comes with a cost elsewhere.

title: Messaging
lesson: A producer sends a message through a broker so a receiver can act later. Decide how long messages live, how delivery is acknowledged and what happens after a failure.
example: A receipt worker acknowledges an email job after sending it. If the worker crashes before acknowledging, another worker may get the same job.
question: A worker receives a job twice after a restart. Which design handles this safely?
answers: Record a stable job ID and guard the side effect against duplicates
Increase how long the broker retains each message
Add another worker to the same subscription
why: Redelivery can occur after a crash. A durable identity lets the handler recognize work it already performed.
detail: Consider the gap between updating a database and publishing a notification. A crash in that gap can leave an order with no event. An outbox stores the pending message in the same database transaction as the order. A separate publisher can resume delivery after a crash, and downstream handlers still need to recognize duplicate events.

terms.definition: A table of pending messages written atomically with the business change that produces them.
A receiver's signal that a delivery reached the agreed stage of processing.

title: Sequential Convoy
lesson: Route messages for the same entity into an ordered group and process that group serially. Independent groups can run at the same time.
example: A parcel's delivery scan must follow its dispatch scan. Grouping by parcel keeps this order, though one very busy parcel can hold up its own group.
question: Orders arrive for thousands of customers. Each customer's updates must keep their original order. How should workers divide work?
answers: Keep each customer's ordered stream on one active consumer at a time
Sort all updates by the time a worker finishes them
Prioritize the smallest update from every customer's stream
why: The customer key defines the boundary for ordering. Different customers can progress independently.
detail: A broker can keep related updates in order if the sender supplies a grouping key and the transport preserves the required order within that group. Include a sequence number when producers can submit updates out of order. If shipment update 8 arrives ahead of update 7, the consumer can pause that shipment and continue processing others.

terms.definition: A value, such as shipment ID, identifying the updates that need coordinated ordering.
A position within an ordered stream that helps a receiver spot missing or repeated updates.

title: Scheduler Agent Supervisor
lesson: A scheduler records the workflow and its current step. Agents perform the remote work, and a supervisor checks deadlines and recovers stalled steps.
example: A media pipeline records when it starts a transcription job. When the deadline passes, the supervisor checks the provider before submitting a duplicate job.
question: A workflow remains marked as running after its worker disappears. Which component should detect the missed deadline?
answers: A supervisor scanning durable step state
A gateway combining the results for the UI
A router selecting the closest worker
why: The supervisor can compare recorded progress with deadlines even after the original worker exits.
detail: Imagine a shipment workflow has completed the address check and started buying postage. The agent stops responding. The supervisor reads the saved step and elapsed time, checks whether a label already exists and then resumes or compensates. Saving the external reference before moving to the next step gives recovery something concrete to check.

terms.definition: A durable record of completed work that allows a workflow to resume.
A follow-up business action that accounts for a previously completed step.

title: Queue-Based Load Leveling
lesson: Put a queue between bursty arrivals and a resource with a fixed safe processing rate. The backlog stores time as well as work, so watch the age of the oldest job.
example: A print shop accepts 600 files at opening and prints 30 per minute. Later arrivals wait behind earlier orders unless the shop changes its scheduling policy.
question: A downstream API permits 20 calls per second. A batch of 1,000 jobs arrives. Which design absorbs the burst?
answers: Buffer jobs and cap the workers' combined call rate
Start a separate worker for every queued job
Retry every refused call immediately
why: The queue holds the spike while the shared rate cap protects the downstream API. Sustained arrivals above capacity still grow the backlog.
detail: Suppose a worker pool finishes 50 jobs each minute and new jobs keep arriving at 30 per minute. A burst that adds 200 waiting jobs takes roughly ten minutes to clear, assuming steady rates. If arrivals rise to 50 per minute, the backlog stays. Choose a maximum waiting time and decide what to do when you exceed it.

terms.definition: The net rate at which a backlog shrinks after subtracting new arrivals from completed jobs.
The time a job has already spent waiting to be processed.

title: Publisher/Subscriber
lesson: A publisher announces an event to a topic. Each interested subscription receives its own delivery, and each subscriber controls how it processes that event.
example: When a book sells, inventory and analytics each consume the sale. An analytics outage can leave that subscription several minutes behind.
question: Billing and analytics must each see every order event. How should they subscribe?
answers: Give each service a separate subscription to the topic
Have both services compete for jobs on one queue
Route odd order IDs to billing and even IDs to analytics
why: Separate subscriptions fan out the same event and track each service's progress independently.
detail: Suppose you add a fraud detector after a shop has already published a year's sales. A new subscription might begin with future events only. If it needs history, the broker must retain events for replay or the service needs a separate backfill. Define the starting point so a backfill and live deliveries do not double-count a sale.

terms.definition: Reading retained events again from a chosen point.
Loading earlier records into a new or repaired view of the data.

title: Priority Queue
lesson: Label jobs by urgency and let the dispatcher prefer higher-priority work. Reserve some capacity for lower priorities if they also have deadlines.
example: A photo service processes live previews ahead of archive exports. A steady flood of previews can otherwise prevent an export from ever starting.
question: High-priority alerts arrive continuously and ordinary alerts never run. What change preserves urgency and makes progress on both?
answers: Give ordinary alerts a guaranteed share of service
Assign a higher priority to every alert
Increase the retention time of ordinary alerts
why: A reserved share or an aging policy bounds starvation while still favoring urgent work.
detail: Priority usually decides which waiting job starts next. If a low-priority export has already occupied the only worker for ten minutes, an urgent alert can still wait behind it. Small work units, separate workers or explicit preemption can help. Choose a policy based on how long an urgent item can afford to wait.

terms.definition: Interrupting running work so a different task can use the resource.
A task waits indefinitely because other tasks repeatedly take precedence.

title: Pipes and Filters
lesson: Split processing into stages with explicit input and output contracts. Connect stages with channels so each stage can change or scale independently.
example: A transcription pipeline decodes audio, transcribes speech and adds timestamps. Separate queues allow more transcription workers but add delivery and tracing overhead.
question: The transcription stage is overloaded while decoding is idle. What advantage does a staged pipeline provide?
answers: Scale the transcription stage independently
Remove the need to track failed audio files
Guarantee every stage processes each file exactly once
why: Each stage has its own capacity. Queued boundaries let one stage absorb work without scaling every other stage.
detail: Follow one failed item through a three-stage image pipeline. If resizing succeeds and watermarking fails, storing the resized image lets the worker retry only the failed stage. Each saved intermediate result costs space and needs an expiry policy. Give stages versioned input formats so a new resize worker can coexist with an older watermark worker.

terms.definition: Output from one processing step that later steps consume.
The input, output and error behavior that neighboring processing steps rely on.

title: Competing Consumers
lesson: Several workers pull from one queue and share the work. A broker normally leases or assigns a delivery to one worker, and can redeliver it after failure.
example: More thumbnail workers can drain a backlog faster until storage bandwidth becomes the bottleneck.
question: Ten identical workers should divide a batch of invoices. Which arrangement fits?
answers: Use one work queue with all ten workers consuming from it
Give each worker a separate subscription to every invoice
Broadcast each invoice to every worker and merge their outputs
why: Consumers on the same queue divide deliveries. Redelivery still calls for duplicate-safe processing.
detail: A worker typically has a deadline to finish a leased message. If processing lasts longer, the broker may offer the same job to another worker while the first is still busy. Size or renew the lease for slow jobs. Monitor repeated failures and move persistently failing jobs aside so they do not occupy all consumers.

terms.definition: The period during which a delivered queue item is temporarily hidden from other consumers.
A separate destination for messages that repeatedly fail normal processing.

title: Choreography
lesson: Services react to domain events and publish the next event as work progresses. The workflow spans several services, so tracing needs a shared business identifier.
example: A reservation event triggers payment. A failed payment event releases the room, but tracing the whole booking now requires correlating multiple events.
question: Booking, payment and inventory react to one another's events. What most helps explain where a booking stopped?
answers: Carry the booking ID through events and record transitions
Give each message an unrelated request ID with no parent
Track only total messages published across all bookings
why: A shared identifier connects independent transitions into the history of a single booking.
detail: Draw the business events as a sequence and assign each one an owner. A ticket service might publish TicketHeld, while payment publishes PaymentAuthorized or PaymentDeclined. Decide who releases a hold if a payment event never arrives. Keeping those decisions explicit makes it possible to change one service without leaving reservations stuck between steps.

terms.definition: A record of a meaningful business fact that has already happened.
An identifier shared by messages or operations belonging to the same workflow.

title: Claim Check
lesson: Store a large payload separately and put a small reference in the message. Receivers use the reference to retrieve the data, so its permissions and lifetime matter.
example: A podcast editor queues a pointer to an audio file. Deleting the file before a delayed worker retries would make that message unusable.
question: A broker accepts 1 MB per message and a video is 500 MB. What should a processing message contain?
answers: A controlled reference to the stored video and its version
The first megabyte of the video and its total length
A longer message retention time and the original video
why: The broker carries a small claim while the object store handles the large bytes. The reference must remain valid through processing.
detail: Consider the two writes involved in sending a large recording. Write the recording successfully before announcing its reference so a worker can always fetch the bytes. If sending the reference fails, the recording can become an orphan. Retain it for retries, track pending publication and clean it up once the recovery window has passed.

terms.definition: The data a message carries or points to for processing.
A stored item that remains after its expected reference or owner is lost.

title: Async Request Reply
lesson: Acknowledge a long operation quickly and return a way to look up its status. Persist job state so the client can reconnect and retrieve the eventual result.
example: A report request returns HTTP 202 and a job URL. Polling too frequently adds traffic, so the client waits between checks.
question: An export takes five minutes and the mobile connection often drops. Which response helps the client resume?
answers: Accept the job and return a durable status URL
Hold the original connection open until the export finishes
Return a success receipt indicating the report is already complete
why: The status resource survives a lost connection and distinguishes acceptance from successful completion.
detail: A job endpoint can return a status document with states such as queued, running, completed and failed. Include an estimate of when to check again, and make the result accessible after completion. A client that loses the initial response may resubmit. Giving the submission an operation ID can connect both attempts to the same job.

terms.definition: A response indicating acceptance for processing while the final outcome is still pending.
Repeatedly checking a resource for a change in status.

title: Data Management
lesson: Choose how records are owned, partitioned, queried and updated. The best shape for writing an event can differ from the shape a screen needs for reading.
example: A shop writes individual sales but serves a precomputed daily total. The dashboard saves query time and can lag behind the most recent sale.
question: A dashboard is expensive because it sums all sales on every visit. Which requirement determines whether a precomputed total fits?
answers: How stale the displayed total may be
How often engineers deploy the web frontend
Which color represents today's sales
why: A precomputed result trades freshness and maintenance work for cheaper reads.
detail: Write down which service can change each fact. A catalog can own a product's current price while a receipt records the price actually charged. Editing the catalog tomorrow should leave yesterday's receipt intact. This example shows why apparently duplicated values sometimes have different meanings and different requirements for consistency and retention.

terms.definition: The authoritative source for a particular fact.
A rule that must hold across valid states, such as a paid invoice matching its recorded total.

title: Static Content Hosting
lesson: Serve prebuilt files directly from object storage or an edge service. Versioned asset names allow long cache lifetimes while a small entry document points to the current release.
example: A puzzle app ships its illustrations as immutable files. Updating an illustration creates a new filename so cached copies of the old one remain safe to use.
question: A release must replace a cached illustration immediately for new visitors. Which approach works with long-lived asset caching?
answers: Publish a versioned file and update the entry document to reference it
Overwrite the file and assume every edge refreshes at once
Set a year-long cache lifetime on the entry document as well
why: A new URL selects the new representation. A fresh entry document tells clients which asset version to request.
detail: A browser first retrieves the page, then follows its links to scripts, images and styles. Publish the new assets before publishing a page that references them. Keep the previous assets available while older pages may still reference them. This release order prevents a visitor who loaded an older page from getting missing files midway through a session.

terms.definition: A fingerprint derived from file contents that can be included in the file name.
The authoritative server or storage location from which an edge cache obtains an asset.

title: Sharding
lesson: Split rows across independent partitions using a shard key. Design for both balanced load and the queries that should stay within one partition.
example: A workspace ID keeps most team queries local. One unusually large workspace can still turn a single shard into a bottleneck.
question: A dataset is evenly sized across shards but one customer dominates traffic. Which measurement reveals the issue?
answers: Request rate and latency per shard
Average record size across the whole database
Number of columns in the shared schema
why: A balanced row count can hide a hot shard. The key must distribute the workload as well as the data.
detail: Range partitioning can make a date-range query cheap because nearby dates live together, but today's shard may receive almost every insert. Hashing a key spreads many distinct keys across shards while making a date-range query harder. List the most frequent queries and the busiest individual keys before committing to a strategy that will be expensive to change.

terms.definition: Assigning contiguous intervals of key values to different partitions.
Sending a query to several partitions and combining their responses.

title: Materialized View
lesson: Store the result of a query in a form ready to serve. Update it as source data changes or rebuild it on a schedule, and account for the gap between updates.
example: A music app precomputes the top songs for each city every hour. Reading a chart is fast, but a new hit may take an hour to appear.
question: A chart tolerates an hour of lag and takes a minute to compute. Which design gives users fast reads?
answers: Refresh a stored chart periodically and serve that result
Run the full aggregation on every chart view
Store only an index of city names
why: The expensive computation moves out of the read path. The refresh interval establishes the expected freshness.
detail: Decide how to handle edits after a summary has been built. If a sale changes from ten dollars to seven, adding seven again inflates the total. A refresh can recompute the affected group or apply the difference once. Keep a way to rebuild the view from its underlying facts when a bug corrupts the summary.

terms.definition: Updating a stored query result using the changes since its last update.
Recomputing the complete result from its source data.

title: Index Table
lesson: Maintain a separate lookup keyed by a field the main store cannot search efficiently. It maps a lookup value to the primary record or its location.
example: Support can look up a ticket by email even though tickets are stored by ID. Changing an email requires keeping the secondary mapping in sync.
question: A key-value database fetches users by ID. Staff need exact email lookups without scanning. What should you add?
answers: A maintained mapping from email to user ID
A separate random shard key for each lookup
A daily count of users grouped by email domain
why: A secondary mapping turns the email into the key the primary store already understands.
detail: When a customer changes an email address, three records may be involved: the user, the new email mapping and the old mapping. If they cannot be changed in one transaction, readers can briefly see stale or missing results. Verify the primary record after lookup and reconcile incomplete index updates. Enforcing globally unique emails needs a separate atomic ownership rule.

terms.definition: A lookup organized by a field other than the record's primary key.
A value or set of values identifying one record in its main store.

title: Event Sourcing
lesson: Represent changes as an ordered history of domain events. Replaying that history reconstructs state, and snapshots can reduce replay time.
example: A points account records earned, spent and expired points. Historical audits become straightforward, but a changed event format must still work during replay.
question: An audit must explain exactly how an account reached its current balance. What should its source of truth preserve?
answers: The ordered business events that changed the balance
Only the latest computed balance
A cache of the last balance displayed to each user
why: Event history preserves the reason and sequence of changes. A projection can derive the current balance.
detail: Two people try to reserve the last studio seat. Each reads the same event stream through version 14. A store that checks the expected version allows one reservation to append version 15. The second writer must reload and reconsider the request. Replaying the history should rebuild state without sending another confirmation email for every past booking.

terms.definition: The stream position a writer believes is current when it submits a change.
A derived representation built by applying events, often optimized for a particular query.

title: CQRS
lesson: Command Query Responsibility Segregation gives writes and reads separate models or interfaces. They can share storage, or use specialized stores with asynchronous updates.
example: A ticket sale checks inventory in the command model. A fast seat map can be slightly behind, so final availability is checked during purchase.
question: A seat map reads from an eventually updated projection. Which component should confirm a seat can be sold?
answers: The command handler enforcing the inventory rule
The browser's last rendered seat map
The asynchronously refreshed popularity ranking
why: The command side owns the invariant. A fast read projection may still show a seat another buyer just claimed.
detail: Separate the verbs from the questions your application answers. ReserveSeat is a command with business rules and a possible rejection. ShowAvailableSeats is a read optimized for browsing. If an asynchronous read model lags, the successful command can return the reservation ID immediately, letting the UI confirm the user's action while the list catches up.

terms.definition: A request to change state that can succeed or be rejected by domain rules.
A request that retrieves information without changing the underlying business state.

title: Cache-Aside
lesson: The application looks in a cache first. On a miss it reads the source, fills the cache and returns the data, then uses expiry or invalidation to manage stale copies.
example: A catalog caches popular product descriptions. A description edit can briefly leave an older copy in the cache.
question: A cached product description changes in the database. What should participate in the update strategy?
answers: Invalidating or refreshing the affected cache entry
Increasing the cache lifetime for every product
Writing the new text only into a browser's memory
why: A cache fill captures one version of the data. Later writes need an explicit freshness strategy.
detail: On a popular item's expiry, many callers can miss at once and send the same query to storage. Coordinate concurrent misses for that key so one caller fetches the value and others share the result. Spread expiration times across popular keys as well. Both choices protect the database when a large batch of cached entries expires.

terms.definition: A surge of simultaneous recomputations or source reads after cached data becomes unavailable.
Combining concurrent equivalent requests into one operation and sharing its result.

title: Design & Implementation
lesson: Choose service boundaries, integration contracts and rollout steps around concrete workloads. Small reversible changes make it easier to measure the effect of a design decision.
example: A team extracts invoice downloads behind an existing URL and can route traffic back during rollout. The proxy adds another component to operate.
question: You must replace one feature of a live monolith while keeping clients working. What is the most useful first boundary?
answers: An existing feature contract whose traffic can be switched independently
A split based only on which files are longest
A new endpoint requiring every client to upgrade simultaneously
why: An independently routable contract supports gradual migration and a practical rollback.
detail: Try writing down a change you expect next month, such as adding a new payment provider. Trace how many modules, databases and client versions would need coordinated changes. If the answer is nearly all of them, a boundary may expose too much detail. Put the translation at one boundary and test the externally observable behavior there.

terms.definition: How strongly a change or failure in one component affects another.
The inputs, outputs and behavior another component can depend on.

title: Strangler Fig
lesson: Route selected capabilities from an existing system to their replacements over time. Migrate ownership of state deliberately so old and new paths agree during the transition.
example: A library moves its search endpoint first and keeps checkout on the old backend. Both systems must keep catalog changes visible until migration ends.
question: A school needs to replace payroll gradually without a single cutover weekend. Which plan fits?
answers: Redirect one capability at a time through a stable facade
Maintain two independent payroll ledgers with unrestricted writes
Wait until every feature is rewritten before sending any production traffic
why: Incremental routing lets the team verify one capability in production and retire the matching legacy piece.
detail: Before switching a feature, capture how the old system handles its trickiest inputs. For reads, a team can quietly query the replacement and compare outputs while returning the old answer. For writes, identify one authoritative writer during each migration step. Routing traffic back is much easier when you know which system owns changes made since the switch.

terms.definition: Sending a copy of a read to a candidate implementation to compare results without affecting the user's response.
The point when production requests or ownership move to the replacement.
A migration pattern that progressively routes pieces of an existing system’s work to its replacement.

title: Sidecar
lesson: Run a helper alongside each application instance, often as a separate container with a shared lifecycle. It can extend the application independently of its language or source code.
example: A local telemetry collector batches logs for every service replica. Each replica also pays the collector's memory cost.
question: A legacy binary cannot be changed but each replica needs a local log forwarder. Where should it run?
answers: In a companion process deployed with each replica
Only in the browser that calls the binary
Inside the source of a shared library the binary must recompile
why: A sidecar supplies a local capability while leaving the application's implementation independent.
detail: Decide how the main process should behave if its helper fails. Losing a metrics exporter may justify dropping telemetry temporarily, while losing a required local proxy may make the replica unable to serve requests. Define separate resource limits and health checks for the helper. A burst of log traffic should have a bounded impact on application memory.

terms.definition: The startup, operation, shutdown and replacement of a component.
A configured ceiling on a component's use of resources such as memory or CPU.
A supporting process deployed alongside an application instance to provide a separate capability.

title: Leader Election
lesson: Select a single instance to coordinate a task for a group. Leases or consensus can transfer leadership after failure, and fencing tokens help storage reject a stale leader.
example: One scheduler closes the daily ledger. A paused former leader might wake up after its lease expires, so the ledger checks the leadership epoch on writes.
question: An expired leader resumes and tries to write after a new leader takes over. What protects the resource?
answers: Reject writes carrying an older fencing token
Assume the previous leader received its shutdown signal
Use the timestamp displayed on the old leader's UI
why: The resource enforces leadership order using a monotonic token. A paused process may still believe it holds a valid lease.
detail: Election gives a group a way to hand off coordination, but actions already started by a previous leader may still reach storage. Attach an epoch number to each protected write and let the receiving resource remember the newest epoch. When a delayed write from epoch 4 arrives after epoch 5 took over, the resource can reject it.

terms.definition: A time-limited grant of authority that must be renewed to remain effective.
A numbered leadership term that advances when control passes to a new holder.

title: Gateway Routing
lesson: Expose one entry point and route requests to the service responsible for each path, host or version. Keep routing rules observable because a bad rule can affect many clients.
example: A store sends /orders to order management and /photos to its media service. Clients keep one host, while the gateway needs redundant capacity.
question: Clients need one hostname while two teams independently move their backend services. Which pattern handles this?
answers: Route requests at a gateway using stable public paths
Send every request to every service and merge the replies
Have every client query both deployment inventories
why: Routing hides backend addresses behind a durable contract and selects the responsible service per request.
detail: For a migration, route a small group of customers to a new implementation while the rest use the old one. If a workflow expects consistent behavior across requests, use a stable customer assignment. Randomly picking a backend on each request could switch the same customer's checkout between incompatible versions halfway through a purchase.

terms.definition: A condition that maps an incoming request to a backend destination.
Exposing a new release to a small group first so its behavior can be measured.

title: Gateway Offloading
lesson: Move common perimeter work such as TLS termination or rate limits into a gateway. Backends still enforce rules that require their own business context.
example: A gateway checks token signatures for five APIs. An order service still verifies that the authenticated buyer owns the requested order.
question: All APIs duplicate TLS setup and token validation. Which change reduces that duplication?
answers: Handle shared edge concerns in a trusted gateway
Place every service's business rules in the mobile app
Combine unrelated API databases into a single schema
why: The gateway can apply common controls consistently while services retain domain-specific authorization.
detail: When the gateway authenticates a caller, a backend needs a trustworthy way to receive that identity. Remove any client-supplied identity header and pass the verified identity over a protected internal connection. Review how the backend behaves when the gateway is unavailable, since moving a shared function also gives many services a shared dependency.

terms.definition: The point that completes the client's encrypted connection before forwarding traffic.
A point where data or identity moves between components with different security assumptions.

title: Gateway Aggregation
lesson: Accept one client request, fetch data from several backends and combine their results. Set deadlines and decide what a partial response looks like when one dependency is slow.
example: A home screen loads a profile, recent orders and recommendations together. It can show core information while recommendations time out.
question: A phone needs three backend responses for one screen over a high-latency connection. What reduces client round trips?
answers: Offer one endpoint that gathers and combines the responses
Send three sequential requests through the same public hostname
Increase image cache lifetimes for all clients
why: Aggregation moves coordination behind the gateway, reducing repeated trips across the mobile network.
detail: Three independent backend calls can often run in parallel. If they take 40, 80 and 300 milliseconds, a response that waits for all three needs at least about 300 milliseconds before network and gateway overhead. Give optional sections their own deadlines and define the response shape when a section is unavailable, so clients can render a useful partial screen.

terms.definition: One incoming operation triggering several outgoing calls.
A response containing the available portions of a result when a dependency fails or times out.

title: External Config Store
lesson: Keep deploy-time or runtime settings in a separate configuration service. Version settings and define what an instance should do if it cannot fetch an update.
example: A search service changes its ranking weights without a binary release. It can keep the last validated settings through a configuration outage.
question: A bad timeout setting spread through the fleet in seconds. Which capability helps recover?
answers: Versioned settings with rollback and staged rollout
Fetching all settings synchronously on every request
Storing the only copy in a single worker's memory
why: Versioning identifies a known-good value. Staged rollout limits how many instances receive a bad update.
detail: Different replicas may observe a configuration change at different moments. For a new event format, enable readers to understand both formats before telling writers to emit the new one. Validate a configuration bundle as a unit and expose its version in diagnostics. Seeing one slow replica on the previous version can explain an otherwise puzzling incident.

terms.definition: The process by which a changed setting reaches the instances using it.
A previously validated settings version retained for fallback.

title: Compute Resource Consolidation
lesson: Place compatible tasks on shared compute so unused capacity does useful work. Measure contention and failure coupling when tasks share the same host.
example: A nightly index build shares a machine with a daytime reporting job. If the build overruns, the two can compete for memory.
question: Which pair is the best candidate to share a host with limited CPU?
answers: Workers whose measured demand peaks at different times
Two latency-critical services that peak together
Jobs that both require all memory continuously
why: Complementary load profiles can improve utilization. Simultaneous peaks increase contention and latency.
detail: A machine with spare CPU can still be short on disk bandwidth. Measure the resources each task needs during its busiest window and leave headroom for spikes. Consolidation also ties maintenance windows together. Restarting the host to patch a batch processor now interrupts anything else sharing it unless the workloads have independent failover.

terms.definition: Capacity deliberately left available for spikes, failures or growth.
Multiple workloads competing for the same finite resource.

title: Backends for Frontend
lesson: Give distinct client experiences tailored backend interfaces. Each backend shapes payloads and calls around its client's needs while shared domain services retain common rules.
example: A watch dashboard receives a tiny activity summary while the web UI loads detailed history. Separate adapters add ownership and maintenance work.
question: A mobile app needs small offline-friendly payloads and a desktop app needs rich drilldowns. What fits?
answers: Provide client-specific backend adapters over shared services
Require both clients to download every domain record
Fork the authoritative business rules into both UIs
why: Client-specific adapters can evolve payloads independently while central services preserve common business behavior.
detail: Look for decisions that genuinely differ between devices. A phone feed may need one small payload with just the first ten items, while a desktop inspector may request richer detail on demand. Both should ask the same underlying service whether an item is visible to this user. Keep display-specific composition close to each client and policy decisions with their owner.

terms.definition: Selecting and structuring fields to fit a client's display or bandwidth needs.
A component that owns business capabilities or rules shared across clients.

title: Anti-Corruption Layer
lesson: Translate between systems that use different domain meanings or contracts. Keep the translation at their boundary so one system's historical conventions stay contained.
example: An old billing system encodes refunds as negative invoices. A new service translates them into explicit refunds and tests the mapping for partial repayments.
question: A legacy field called customer means a household, while a new model uses individual people. What belongs at the boundary?
answers: An adapter with explicit identity and meaning mappings
A transparent forwarder that only renames the field
One global customer ID assigned without resolving household membership
why: The mismatch is semantic. A translation layer must preserve the meaning of the data in each domain.
detail: Model the awkward cases before mapping fields. If a legacy booking status of closed can mean either canceled or completed, a translation may need an additional timestamp or an explicit unknown outcome. Silently picking one interpretation loses information. Give the boundary tests for ambiguous historical records as well as the obvious current ones.

terms.definition: Translation that preserves the meaning of a value across two different models.
A component that converts one interface or representation into another.

title: Ambassador
lesson: Place a local proxy beside a client to handle calls to remote services. It can centralize connection management, discovery or telemetry for applications using different languages.
example: A native worker calls a local proxy that manages remote service connections. The extra hop simplifies the worker but adds a dependency on the proxy.
question: Several old applications need a consistent outbound connection policy without code changes. What should they call?
answers: A local ambassador proxy that connects on their behalf
A separate data warehouse for request history
A gateway that handles only inbound public requests
why: An ambassador owns the outbound path and can apply a common policy for heterogeneous clients.
detail: Consider which component owns a timeout or retry. If the application makes three attempts and its local proxy makes three attempts for each call, the remote service might see nine requests. Agree on one retry budget across the layers. Record both the application's request ID and the proxy's attempts so operators can trace failures.

terms.definition: A component that forwards requests initiated by an application to remote destinations.
A limit on repeat attempts or the additional load they may generate.

title: Reliability Patterns
lesson: Define what successful service means over time, including lost work and recovery time. Identify a likely failure and decide how to contain, tolerate or recover from it.
example: A booking service can survive losing a worker if it durably records accepted reservations. Waiting for durable storage adds latency to acknowledgement.
question: You promise to preserve every accepted reservation through a worker restart. When should the service acknowledge acceptance?
answers: After durably recording the reservation
As soon as it enters a worker's in-memory queue
When the load balancer receives the first byte
why: The acknowledgement creates a user-visible promise. Durable state makes recovery possible after the worker disappears.
detail: Pick an operation such as saving a draft and ask where an accepted edit could disappear. Follow it through the browser, network, API and storage. At each handoff, ask who still holds a recoverable copy. An explicit answer guides the choice of local persistence, acknowledgement timing or duplicate handling much better than adding redundancy everywhere.

terms.definition: A specific way a component or operation can fail.
The ability of acknowledged data to survive the failures the design promises to tolerate.

title: Availability
lesson: Availability measures whether a service fulfills its contract when needed. Define success from the user's perspective and include a time limit if late answers are unusable.
example: A search endpoint can return HTTP 200 after a full minute. For a two-second search objective, that request still missed the target.
question: An API reports 100% process uptime but users experience timeouts. Which measure captures their experience?
answers: Fraction of valid requests completed successfully within the deadline
Count of running processes in the cluster
Number of deployments without rollback
why: User-facing success measures the actual operation through its dependencies and time budget.
detail: Suppose an endpoint receives 100,000 eligible requests over a week and promises 99.9% success. That allows 100 failures under this request-based measure. A short outage during peak traffic can consume more of that allowance than a longer outage at night. Choose the denominator carefully and separately inspect important low-volume user journeys.

terms.definition: An observed measure of service behavior, such as the fraction of successful requests.
The amount of failure permitted by a service's objective over a stated period.

title: Deployment Stamps
lesson: Deploy repeatable, independently operated copies of a service stack. Assign customers or partitions to stamps so a failure or rollout touches a bounded group.
example: A school platform puts groups of districts on separate stamps. A small district avoids another stamp's outage, while operating many stacks raises cost.
question: One bad release should reach only a small group of tenants initially. Which rollout fits?
answers: Deploy to one independent tenant stamp and observe it
Update every stamp's shared database schema destructively first
Switch all tenant traffic to the updated stamp at once
why: A stamp provides a bounded deployment unit when its critical dependencies are isolated as well.
detail: A routing directory can map each tenant to its assigned stamp. Capacity planning now happens per stamp, so track tenant size and leave space for growth. A bug in a global routing directory can still affect every stamp. Verify that apparently independent copies can keep serving existing tenants when their shared provisioning tools are unavailable.

terms.definition: The portion of a system or user population affected by one failure.
The rule or mapping that assigns a customer's workload to a particular deployment.

title: Geodes
lesson: Run regional copies of the stack that can serve users from multiple locations. Route requests to a suitable healthy region and plan how data reaches the others.
example: A traveler can use a nearby region for low-latency reads. Replicating their writes worldwide introduces either delay or coordination cost.
question: A regional app must keep serving travelers after one region fails. What does a geode arrangement require?
answers: Healthy alternate regions with the data and capacity to serve those users
A DNS alias pointing to another name for the same failed server
A global dashboard listing every regional process
why: Traffic redirection works only when the destination can process the request and access the necessary state.
detail: Imagine two regions both accept a profile update while the network between them is down. Local writes can keep the application responsive, but the design needs a rule for reconciling competing changes later. A single write authority avoids that conflict and may make writes unavailable from a disconnected region. Choose based on what the field actually represents.

terms.definition: An arrangement in which several sites serve live traffic at the same time.
The rule that reconciles competing changes made to the same data.

title: Health Endpoint Monitoring
lesson: Expose a lightweight signal that probes can check regularly. A readiness check guides routing, while a liveness check can signal that restarting the process might help.
example: A new catalog replica stays unready until its local index loads. Using that same check for liveness could restart it repeatedly during startup.
question: A process is alive but its index is still loading. What should its readiness probe tell the router?
answers: Keep this replica out of the serving pool for now
Restart every replica sharing the same index version
Send it all traffic so the index warms faster
why: Readiness controls traffic admission. A temporary startup condition can resolve without restarting the process.
detail: A deep check that always queries a shared database can turn a database outage into every replica reporting unready at once. Separate process health, the ability to accept traffic and external end-to-end testing. Put a small time budget on probes and avoid expensive work in each probe, since the probes continue during incidents.

terms.definition: Whether an instance is currently suitable to receive normal traffic.
A scheduled test request that exercises a service from an observer's perspective.

title: Throttling
lesson: Set limits on how quickly or concurrently clients consume a scarce resource. Signal temporary limits to callers and leave capacity for other tenants.
example: A report API caps each tenant's simultaneous exports. A tenant may wait longer, while its neighbors keep their interactive response times.
question: One customer's exports consume all database connections. Which targeted control protects other customers?
answers: Apply a per-tenant export concurrency limit
Offer the customer unlimited immediate retries
Keep idle export connections open longer
why: A concurrency limit bounds one tenant's active resource consumption even when individual jobs last a long time.
detail: A token bucket separates a short burst allowance from the longer-term rate. A bucket that holds 20 tokens and refills at five per second can accept 20 one-token calls immediately when full. Once depleted, callers wait for the refill. Limit concurrent work separately if a few long jobs can occupy all connections despite a low arrival rate.

terms.definition: A limiter that adds permits at a configured rate up to a maximum stored balance.
The number of operations in progress at the same time.

title: High Availability
lesson: Design redundant components and failover paths so a single expected failure need not interrupt service for long. Check shared dependencies and test that standby capacity can really take traffic.
example: Two web replicas on one host can survive a process crash. Losing the host takes out both, so a host-level objective requires another failure domain.
question: Two redundant servers use the same power circuit. Which change targets a circuit outage?
answers: Place serving capacity in independent power failure domains
Run a second copy of the application on each server
Poll the shared circuit twice as often
why: Redundancy helps against failures that spare at least one usable path. A common power dependency defeats both servers.
detail: An alternate zone needs enough spare capacity to take traffic during a failure. Three zones running at 80% of equal capacity cannot carry their full combined load using only two zones. For that failure plan, reserve capacity, scale quickly enough, or decide which work can be shed. Exercise the transition under realistic traffic.

terms.definition: Switching service from an unavailable component or location to a surviving one.
A group of resources that can be lost together through one event.

title: Bulkhead
lesson: Reserve separate resource pools for different workloads or dependencies. Exhaustion in one pool then leaves capacity for the others, at the cost of sometimes leaving capacity idle.
example: A slow recommendation provider fills its own connection pool. Checkout still has a separate budget to contact payments.
question: Slow image requests consume all worker slots and block account updates. Which design isolates them?
answers: Give image and account work separate bounded worker pools
Expand the single shared queue without a limit
Increase the timeout on every image job
why: A separate pool places a hard boundary on how many slots image work can consume.
detail: Allocate pools around what must survive a failure. Giving each tenant its own queue helps little if every queue drains into a single unbounded shared database pool. Follow requests to the next scarce resource, then enforce a matching admission budget there. Track rejected work by pool to see whether an allocation needs adjusting.

terms.definition: Deciding whether to start new work given current limits.
A separation that limits how a failure or resource shortage spreads.
Isolation of capacity into separate pools so exhaustion of one pool leaves others usable.

title: Circuit Breaker
lesson: Track failures for a dependency and temporarily stop sending normal calls when the failure threshold is reached. After a cooldown, allow a small trial to test recovery.
example: A map provider times out repeatedly, so the app immediately shows a saved address. While open, the breaker may skip calls that would have succeeded.
question: A provider has timed out for several minutes and each attempt ties up a worker. Which action should an open breaker take?
answers: Fail fast or use a fallback while allowing controlled recovery probes later
Send each new request with several immediate retries
Hold all workers until the provider recovers
why: Failing fast releases local resources. Limited probes discover recovery without flooding the dependency.
detail: Measure enough calls to tell a real outage from a single unlucky request. A breaker can open after a sustained failure rate, wait, then permit a limited number of trial calls. Decide which errors should count. A caller's invalid input usually says little about whether the dependency can serve its next valid request.

terms.definition: The period when a breaker blocks ordinary calls to a dependency.
A trial period when a breaker admits limited calls to evaluate recovery.
A mechanism that temporarily stops calls to a failing dependency and later probes for recovery.

title: Resiliency
lesson: Prepare to recover useful behavior after disruption. Recovery time and recovery point objectives describe how long an interruption may last and how much recent data loss is tolerable.
example: A journal app can restore yesterday's backup quickly, yet still lose a day's entries. More frequent durable copies reduce that gap at extra cost.
question: Your service recovers in five minutes but loses an hour of accepted edits. Which target measures that loss window?
answers: Recovery point objective
Recovery time objective
Median request latency
why: The recovery point objective measures tolerable data loss in time. Recovery time measures how long restoration takes.
detail: Practice restoring into an empty environment and then try opening a real record. A completed backup job alone cannot show that the restored data, schema, credentials and application work together. Time the entire exercise and inspect how recent the last recovered record is. These measurements turn a recovery promise into something the team can test.

terms.definition: A rehearsal that checks whether a recovery procedure produces a usable service.
The latest point in the data history that a recovery procedure restores.

title: Compensating Transaction
lesson: When several services commit separate steps, a later failure can require new actions that offset earlier steps. Persist progress and make compensations safe to retry.
example: A rail ticket is booked before a hotel rejects a package. Canceling the ticket may incur a fee, so the compensation follows the actual refund policy.
question: A package purchase fails after a partner has already issued a ticket. How should the workflow recover?
answers: Record and run the partner's cancellation or refund operation
Roll back only the local package database and assume the ticket disappears
Replay the entire purchase with a new booking ID
why: The partner committed independent state. A compensating business action reconciles that state according to the partner's rules.
detail: A refund can be interrupted too. Store a record of which reversals remain and give each one a stable operation ID so a restarted worker can continue safely. Decide which steps require human review, such as a partner refusing cancellation. Show the user a pending resolution state while the system still has business work to complete.

terms.definition: A distributed business workflow composed of local transactions and recovery actions.
A corrective action that can be repeated without applying the correction twice.

title: Retry
lesson: Repeat an operation after a temporary failure within a deadline and attempt budget. Backoff and jitter spread attempts over time, and a stable operation key can protect side effects.
example: A payment response times out after the bank may have charged the card. Retrying with the same idempotency key lets the provider recognize that payment.
question: A charge request times out with an unknown outcome. What makes a retry safer?
answers: Reuse a provider-supported idempotency key for that charge
Generate a distinct purchase ID on every attempt
Keep retrying instantly until a response arrives
why: The same operation identity lets the provider return or complete the original charge without creating another.
detail: Fit each attempt inside the user's total deadline. If a request has 500 milliseconds left, waiting a full second for a retry cannot help that caller. Classify failures as temporary or permanent, space temporary attempts apart and cap their count. A small randomized delay reduces the chance of thousands of clients trying again at the same instant.

terms.definition: Increasing the delay between successive attempts.
Random variation added to retry timing to spread traffic over time.

title: Security
lesson: Identify who can call a system, which actions each identity can perform and where sensitive data travels. Apply controls at the point where a protected action takes place.
example: A notes API verifies a signed-in user and checks ownership before reading a private note. That extra lookup protects against exposing another user's note.
question: Two users are signed in. What should the API check before returning a private document by ID?
answers: Whether this user is authorized to read this document
Whether the document ID has a valid format
Whether this user signed in within the past day
why: Authentication identifies the caller. Resource-specific authorization determines whether that caller may read the document.
detail: Start with one valuable action, such as exporting a workspace. Identify the caller, the workspace, the requested operation and where permissions are checked. Record a useful audit event when the export starts, and limit access to the resulting file as well. Protecting the request alone leaves a gap if its output can be fetched by anyone.

terms.definition: An identifiable actor, such as a person or service, whose permissions can be checked.
Granting only the access required for the intended task and duration.

title: Federated Identity
lesson: Trust an external identity provider to authenticate a user and issue a verifiable assertion or token. Your service validates the token and decides what the identity may access locally.
example: A university app accepts campus sign-in. Disabling an account at the provider can take time to affect previously issued tokens, depending on their lifetime.
question: A campus login token has a valid signature but names a different application as its audience. What should your app do?
answers: Reject the token because it was issued for another audience
Accept it because both applications trust the campus provider
Use the username alone to create a local session
why: Audience validation binds an assertion to its intended recipient. A valid signature alone does not grant access to every trusting app.
detail: A service can identify a user using both the provider's identity and the user's stable subject identifier. An email address can change or be reassigned and may be ambiguous across providers. Validate the token for the chosen protocol, including its intended audience and lifetime, then map that authenticated identity to permissions in the application.

terms.definition: The authority that created an identity assertion or token.
The identifier the issuer assigns to the user or other principal represented by a token.

title: Gatekeeper
lesson: Place a controlled entry service in front of a protected backend to check incoming requests. Restrict direct backend access so callers cannot bypass those checks.
example: A file-processing API admits validated requests from a gateway over a private network. The gateway needs its own redundancy to avoid becoming a common failure point.
question: A gateway validates requests, but a backend also accepts direct public calls. What closes this gap?
answers: Restrict backend ingress to the trusted path and authorized callers
Add more validation messages to the gateway response
Increase the cache lifetime of the backend address
why: The protection applies only when requests pass through the enforced checks. Ingress policy makes that boundary effective.
detail: Keep validation at the front door inexpensive enough to apply under load. For a document conversion service, check the caller's permission and allowed request size before assigning a costly conversion worker. The worker still verifies the document conditions it understands. Give the entry service only the access it needs to send accepted jobs onward.

terms.definition: Traffic entering a service or network boundary.
Using several independent protections so one missed check does not expose the entire system.

title: Valet Key
lesson: After checking permission, issue a short-lived credential scoped to one resource and action. The client can then transfer data directly without routing the bytes through your application.
example: A photo app signs a five-minute upload URL for one object. Anyone holding a usable URL may exercise its permissions until it expires.
question: A user should upload one profile picture directly to storage. Which credential fits?
answers: A short-lived write permission scoped to that user's target object
A permanent account-wide storage key
A read-only link to the whole photo bucket
why: The credential needs just the intended operation, object and time window. Direct transfer keeps the file bytes off the app server.
detail: Choose a unique object name before issuing an upload grant, then verify completion before adding the image to a public gallery. A grant to upload bytes says nothing about whether the resulting image is valid. Keep its expiry long enough for the transfer and short enough to limit exposure if the URL is shared accidentally.

terms.definition: A URL containing a verifiable, scoped grant to perform an operation on a resource.
The time after which a credential is no longer accepted for new requests.
